chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, the compiler of this book, said:

I saw his tomb in the place he mentioned. A wall was erected at its face, and the mosque's mihrab was there. Beside it was a door leading to the tomb's location in a narrow, dark room. We used to enter it and visit him monthly. This was my practice from when I entered Baghdad in the year 408 until the year 432. Then the chief Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn al-Faraj demolished that wall, exposed the tomb to view, and built a sepulcher over it. It is under a ceiling, and anyone who wishes can enter and visit it. The neighborhood residents seek blessing by visiting him and say he is a virtuous man. Sometimes they say: he is the son of the wet-nurse of Husain (peace be upon him), though they do not know the true reality about him. This condition continues to this day, which is the year 447, as it is.
ai.seo_question: What is the historical description of the Special Emissary's tomb in Baghdad according to Shaykh al-Tusi?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi documents the physical evolution of the tomb of the Special Emissary (likely Muhammad ibn Abi 'Aqil) in Baghdad, noting its transition from a concealed, dark chamber to an accessible shrine with a wooden coffin. He highlights the local populace's veneration of the site, reflecting their belief in the individual's righteousness and his familial connection to the Ahl al-Bayt, even if the precise identity remained a subject of local tradition rather than definitive historical record.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: I saw his tomb in that place. A wall was erected at its face at which the mosque’s Mihrab (niche) stood. On its side is a gate that goes to the tomb in a dark and small room. We used to enter that room and visit him every month. Such was my practice during my stay in Baghdad, from year four hundred and eight, until four hundred and thirty and something. Then the Chief Abu Mansur Muhammad Ibn Faraj tore down that wall and manifested the tomb to view and built a sepulcher over it. It is under a ceiling and anyone who desires can enter and visit it. The neighbors seek blessing by visiting him and believe that he is a virtuous man. They often say he is the son of the woman who raised the Doyen of the Martyrs Husain (a.s) and do not know the reality about him. This condition continues until this day of ours, which is the year four hundred and forty seven.
